{{Short description|American mathematician (born 1938)}}
{{other people||Robert Berger (disambiguation){{!}}Robert Berger}}

'''Robert Berger''' (born 1938) is an applied mathematician, known for discovering the first [[aperiodic tiling]]<ref name="Darling2004">{{cite book|last=Darling|first=David J.|authorlink=David J. Darling|title=The universal book of mathematics: from Abracadabra to Zeno's paradoxes|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0YiXM-x--4wC&pg=PA18|access-date=29 September 2011|year=2004|publisher=John Wiley and Sons|isbn=978-0-471-27047-8|pages=18–}}</ref> using a set of 20,426 distinct tile shapes.

==Contributions to tiling theory==
The unexpected existence of aperiodic tilings, although not Berger's explicit construction of them, follows from another result proved by Berger: that the so-called [[domino problem]] is [[Undecidable problem|undecidable]], disproving a conjecture of [[Hao Wang (academic)|Hao Wang]], Berger's advisor.  The result is analogous to a 1962 construction used by [[Andrew Kahr|Kahr]], [[Edward F. Moore|Moore]], and Wang, to show that a more constrained version of the domino problem was undecidable.<ref>{{cite journal|journal = [[Mathematical Reviews]] | volume = 36 | number = 49 | last = Büchi | first = J. R. | authorlink = Julius Richard Büchi | title = The undecidability of the domino problem | mr = 0216954 }}</ref>

==Education and career==
Berger did his undergraduate studies at [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]], and studied [[applied physics]] at [[Harvard]], earning a master's degree, before shifting to applied mathematics for his doctorate. Along with Hao Wang,  Berger's other two doctoral committee members were [[Patrick Carl Fischer]] and [[Marvin Minsky]]. Later, he has worked in the Digital Integrated Circuits Group of the [[Lincoln Laboratory]].<ref>Author biography from {{citation|url=http://www.ll.mit.edu/publications/journal/pdf/vol02_no1/2.1.5.neuromorphicsystems.pdf|title=A generic architecture for wafer-scale neuromorphic systems|first1=J. I.|last1=Raffel|first2=J. R.|last2=Mann|first3=R.|last3=Berger|first4=A. M.|last4=Soares|first5=S.|last5=Gilbert|journal=The Lincoln Laboratory Journal|volume=2|issue=1|year=1989|pages=63–76|bibcode=1989LLabJ...2...63R |access-date=2011-09-30|archive-date=2012-05-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120521070429/http://www.ll.mit.edu/publications/journal/pdf/vol02_no1/2.1.5.neuromorphicsystems.pdf|url-status=dead}}.</ref>

==Publications==
Berger's work on tiling was published as "The Undecidability of the Domino Problem" in the ''[[Memoirs of the AMS]]'' in 1966.<ref name=Berger>{{citation |last=Berger |first=Robert |title=The Undecidability of the Domino Problem |journal=[[Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=66 |year=1966 |issue=66 |page=72 pp|doi=10.1090/memo/0066|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8AmiHD0Lbu8C&q=%22Robert+Berger%22+%22The+undecidability+of+the+domino+problem%22&pg=PA1|url-access=subscription }}.</ref> This paper is essentially a reprint of Berger's 1964 dissertation at [[Harvard University]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=Robert Berger|id=114475}}.</ref>

In 2009, a paper by Berger and other Lincoln Laboratories researchers, "Wafer-scale 3D integration of InGaAs image sensors with Si readout circuits", won the best paper award at the IEEE International 3D System Integration Conference (3DIC).<ref>Awards and Recognition, [http://www.ll.mit.edu/publications/Annual_Report_2010.pdf Lincoln Laboratory Annual Report 2010], p. 50, retrieved 2011-09-30.</ref> In 2010, a [[CMOS]] [[infrared]] imaging device with an [[analog-to-digital converter]] in each pixel, coinvented by Berger, was one of ''R&D Magazine'''s [[R&D 100 Award]] recipients.<ref>[http://www.ll.mit.edu/news/R_D100s.html MIT Lincoln Laboratory receives five R&D 100 Awards], Lincoln Laboratory, retrieved 2011-09-30.</ref>
